#9878. $1 of GPT-5.1 tokens finds new ways around China’s Great Firewall

PLUS: Lenovo's infra group finally makes big profit; Indonesia’s glaciers are gone; Australian bank releases its AI bug-finder; and more!

Researchers have found new ways to evade China’s Great Firewall after spending just $1 worth of tokens.

That result appeared last week in a paper titled “CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models” presented at the Conference on Computer and Communications Security run by the Association for Computing Machinery’s Special Interest Group on Security, Audit and Control.

Penned by six researchers from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, University of Colorado Boulder, and activist group the Great Firewall Report, the paper points out that finding holes in the Great Firewall is a laborious process – so just the kind of task worth handing to AI.

The authors came up with a tool they call “CircumVolve” and describe as “a system for automated discovery of censorship circumvention strategies across the full network stack.”

“CircumVolve combines LLM code generation with iterative feedback-driven evaluation to produce verifiable and deployable evasion techniques,” they wrote. “CircumVolve models different censorship techniques as discrete scenarios, each capturing the specific context, protocol constraints, and blocking mechanisms of real-world censors. Within each scenario, evasion strategies are represented as executable Python programs that implement packet and protocol manipulations — from rewriting TCP/IP header fields, to crafting DNS queries that exploit parser ambiguities, to modifying the internal structure of encrypted QUIC Initial packets — while maintaining protocol correctness within tolerable bounds or strategically violating it when beneficial.”

The authors tested CircumVolve on simulated censorship tools used by China, Iran, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan, and on virtual private servers deployed on clouds in those countries. Those tests found the median API cost to the first successful evasion was less than $1 in token expenditure costs when using GPT-5.1.

The authors acknowledge that operators of censorship infrastructure might be able to observe CircumVolve at work, but feel its relatively small payloads – 80 KB of outgoing and 150 KB of incoming traffic – and 25-45-second pauses between tests might see it fly under the radar.

“CircumVolve represents a first step in leveraging LLMs to accelerate the censorship-circumvention lifecycle,” the authors wrote. “By automating the labor-intensive tasks of protocol analysis, implementation, and testing, AI-driven approaches make studying circumvention capabilities far more accessible to the comparatively under-resourced Internet freedom community [and] demonstrates how AI-assisted systems can narrow the resource gap between Internet freedom advocates and well-funded censoring states.”

Ever since acquiring IBM’s x86 server business in 2014, Chinese hardware giant Lenovo has struggled to turn a profit from datacenter sales, even as it expanded its business into storage, networking, and selling to hyperscalers.

The AI boom has finally done what various strategy shifts and waves of hype could not: propel the company’s Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) to a $1 billion quarterly profit.

In its Q2 results announcement [PDF] last week, the company revealed ISG revenue hit a quarterly record of $11.3 billion, up 178 percent year-over-year, and that lovely big profit. At a time when enterprise hardware supply chains are tight, Lenovo says it was able to increase shipments of x86 servers and even emerge as the largest vendor of such systems with 16 percent market share.

Lenovo also claimed it’s moved further ahead as the planet’s premier PC provider, by pointing to 15 percent year-on-year growth for its intelligent devices group where quarterly revenue reached $17.4 billion. The company claims it has 23.8 percent of the PC market and now has seven percent more market share than its closest rival, Apple. The company said premium devices account for 63 percent of its PC business

Overall revenue rose 48 percent year over year to $30.24 billion for the quarter.

It may surprise readers to know that Indonesia, the nation that spreads across 17,000 islands in the tropical latitudes of 11°S to 6°N, is home to alpine regions sufficiently high that glaciers can form.

Indonesia’s glaciers clung to the top of Puncak Jaya, aka Carstenz Pyramid, a 4,884-meter peak on New Guinea at 4°S.

Sadly, an assessment published last week by NASA says the glaciers have probably melted to the point at which not much is left other than a few patches of ice.

NASA last week posted images that show glaciers covering 4.31 km2 atop Puncak Jaya in 1988, and another from this year that shows most of that ice is gone. Images from September 2025 apparently showed just .09km2 of ice remained.

“To qualify as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to be thick enough to flow downhill under its own weight, and it needs an area where snow builds up faster than it melts,” NASA’s Kathryn Hansen wrote. “Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows.”

For what it’s worth, commercial operators run expeditions to Puncak Jaya. Peak-baggers seek it out because some consider it the highest mountain in Australasia/Oceania and therefore one of the “Seven Summits” –  the highest point on each continent.

The Reg won’t get into the debate about the validity of including Puncak Jaya on that list, but if you fancy some equatorial alpine action your correspondent recently climbed Malaysia’s 4,095m Mount Kinabalu. It’s an overnight walk that requires no technical skills or gear, but definitely demands supple knees. The peak was clearly glaciated in the distant past but snow is now extremely rare on Kinabalu.

Here’s an odd one: Australia’s Commonwealth Bank (CBA) created an AI-powered tool to scan its bespoke code for bugs, and has now packaged it as a free release called “CodeCheck.”

The bank says analyzes the output of OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code with “a consistent process for analyzing code, investigating potential vulnerabilities and providing information to assist engineers.” Apparently, it is “ based on an approach used within CBA, but it is not the same as, and does not represent, the systems, tools or controls CBA uses internally.”

The bank posted CodeCheck to GitHub, where it warns the project is “a one-time open-source release for businesses to evaluate” and that it will not actively maintain, update, or support the code.

Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) last week announced it has reached an agreement with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) to take over responsibility for running launches of its flagship H3 rocket when used in certain configurations.

The deal means MHI will handle launches for H3s that use a pair of LE-9 liquid-fuel engines alongside two SRB-3 solid-fuel boosters.

JAXA will continue running launches that use different, or experimental, configurations.

Once JAXA is satisfied those new rigs are reliable, it plans to transition them to private operators, too. ®

#9877. Amazon S3 Tables now support all Apache Iceberg V3 data types

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Amazon S3 Tables now support all data types in the Apache Iceberg V3 specification. You can create V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables to take advantage of V3 features like deletion vectors, row lineage, and new data types such as variant, nanosecond timestamps, unknown, geometry, and geography.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for managing large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data in open Parquet files in data lakes on object storage like Amazon S3. Amazon S3 Tables offer storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with fully managed features like automatic compaction, maintenance, replication, and Intelligent-Tiering.

Teams running analytics on Apache Iceberg V2 tables often hit the same limits as their data grows. A compliance request to delete 50,000 user records from a 2-billion-row table leaves behind positional delete files that slow queries until compaction runs. Semi-structured events land as JSON strings that every query has to parse. Geospatial coordinates and nanosecond-precision timestamps get encoded as strings or integers. Each workaround adds storage cost, query latency, and pipeline code. With V3, Iceberg solves these challenges by offering native support for semi-structured and geospatial data, faster row-level operations, and built-in row lineage for data governance.

Starting today, Amazon S3 Tables support all V3 data types, including variant, nanosecond timestamps, geometry, geography, and unknown, along with deletion vectors and row lineage. You can create new V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables in place, and S3 Tables continue to run compaction and maintenance for you.

Apache Iceberg V3 V3 is the latest version of the Iceberg specification. Among its many improvements, V3 introduces capabilities that address the most common pain points in V2. This includes:

Deletion vectors replace V2’s positional delete files with a compact binary format. That 50,000-row compliance delete now writes a single deletion vector file instead of thousands of small deletes, significantly reducing compaction time and delete file overhead.

Row lineage adds _row_id and _last_updated_sequence_number to each record automatically. Your downstream pipelines can query these fields to find changed rows without scanning the full table.

New data types let you store semi-structured, geospatial, and nanosecond-precision data natively instead of encoding it as strings or integers:

Variant data type stores semi-structured data in columnar format. During writes, the engine shreds variant data into hidden columns and collects statistics. At query time, those statistics enable file pruning that significantly reduces I/O compared to parsing JSON strings.

The following sections walk through how to use these V3 capabilities in practice, with examples that show how to create tables, work with the new data types, and manage data at scale.

Getting started A retail analytics team tracks user behavior across web and mobile apps. Each event has a different structure: page views include URLs and duration, purchases include items and amounts, and searches include query terms and result counts. With V3’s variant type, you store all event shapes in one table without predefined schemas:

Insert events with different payload shapes without worrying about schema evolution:

Now query the variant column directly, without PARSE_JSON at read time. With Amazon EMR Spark, use variant_get:

To enable deletion vectors for write operations, configure merge-on-read mode:

Now when you run a compliance delete, V3 writes a small deletion vector instead of rewriting data files:

S3 Tables compaction handles these deletion vector files automatically on the next maintenance cycle.

Upgrading from V2 AWS provides backwards compatibility for both versions to minimize disruption during migration to V3. Existing V2 readers continue to work on upgraded tables until you’re ready to fully adopt V3 features. For more details, see the S3 Tables Iceberg V3 documentation. Upgrade an existing table atomically without rewriting data:

On the next compaction cycle, S3 Tables remove old V2 delete files. New modifications use deletion vectors automatically. Row lineage fields initialize on the first data modification after the upgrade.

This is a one-way operation. The Apache Iceberg specification does not support downgrading from V3 to V2. Verify that all engines accessing the table support V3 before upgrading.

Using row lineage for incremental pipelines After your table has V3 data, use row lineage to build efficient incremental pipelines:

This returns only rows modified after sequence number 42. Your downstream jobs can checkpoint this value and process only new changes on each run, instead of scanning the full table.

Compatibility across AWS analytics services AWS offers the broadest native Apache Iceberg support of any major cloud provider, with Iceberg-compatible services at every layer of the data stack: ingestion, storage, catalog, and analytics. You can store and automatically optimize V3 tables in Amazon S3 Tables, write data with Amazon EMR Spark, integrate and manage data with AWS Glue, and run analytics with Amazon Redshift. To learn more about AWS analytics support for V3, see the Apache Iceberg on AWS prescriptive guidance.

Both S3 Tables and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) API, enabling interoperability across engines regardless of the catalog endpoint.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables support for all Apache Iceberg V3 data types is now available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables are supported. Apache Iceberg V3 support is available at no additional charge; standard S3 Tables pricing applies.

To get started, visit the Amazon S3 Tables documentation or create a table bucket from the Amazon S3 console. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Send feedback to AWS re:Post or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#9875. Announcing AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered intelligence to optimize your cloud environment (preview)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing the public preview of AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered service that analyzes your AWS environment to deliver targeted, contextual recommendations for improving your applications’ cost, security, performance, and resilience. The AWS Well-Architected Agent analyzes your infrastructure, understands unique business goals, and delivers contextual recommendations with ready-to-implement fixes. It delivers context-aware optimization without relying on manual audits or generic checklists.

The agent evaluates your environment as an experienced cloud architect would. It automatically correlates utilization metrics, resource configurations, and application topology, and analyzes against Well-Architected best practices across 65+ AWS services. It generates recommendations aligned to your declared business goals, delivers implementation packages with every finding, and surfaces cross-pillar trade-offs making it simpler to remediate the findings.

Here are the three main features of this service:

AWS Well-Architected Agent in action To get started, create an agent profile to define the scope of what Well-Architected Agent can access and provide recommendations on, complete the IAM role setup to access resources, conduct architecture review, and remediate recommendations.

Create an agent profile In the AWS Well-Architected console, choose Get started with Well-Architected Agent. You can define an agent profile that specifies which AWS accounts and applications to monitor, which optimization pillars to focus on, and the permissions required.

You can choose AWS accounts or AWS Regions to monitor and optimization pillars that matter most to your business. You can also set goals for each pillar: cost optimization, performance, resilience, and security.

To give access to the agent for your AWS environment, provision customer-managed IAM roles the agent uses to read resource configurations, utilization metrics, and application topology. To learn more, visit the IAM prerequisite for AWS Well-Architected Agent.

When you choose Get Started, the agent creates your agent profile. Resource and application recommendations will be generated within 24 hours after profile creation.

You can conduct an architecture review on pre-deployment workloads by uploading an IaC project in Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) to be analyzed. Choose Conduct architecture review in the dashboard, upload a.zip file containing IaC project or repository file, and select which Well-Architected lens to use for reviewing your infrastructure.

You can define your applications to add context which will enhance the relevancy and further contextualize recommendations. Choose Add application context in the dashboard, add your applications with AWS accounts, AWS Regions, AWS services, tags if you want to narrow the scope to specific resources, and the details of applications.

Review prioritized recommendations and start remediating Now you can see generated prioritized recommendations generated by the agent across your resources and applications, selected pillars, ranked against your declared goals, with automation-ready remediation included.

When you choose the specific recommendation, you can see the details, insights into why the agent are suggesting the recommendation, impacts and trade-off, and recommended fixes across affected AWS resources.

Choose Start remediation to address recommended fixes. You can choose the console, updated IaC template, CLI commands to remediate by the resolution type. It provides detailed step-by-step instructions and you can roll out this instruction and verify the result.

When you choose Using updated IaC template, the agent provides the code changes needed to update your existing IaC templates such as the CDK function shown above which you can copy directly into your codebase.

You can also configure API access to integrate recommendations directly into your existing development and operations workflows. To interact with the agent programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the AWS Well-Architected Agent documentation.

Things to know Here are some things that you should know about the Well-Architected Agent.

You can still use existing AWS Well-Architected Tool to manually evaluate your cloud architecture with user-defined lenses that measure your workload using your own best practices.

Join the preview Access to the AWS Well-Architected Agent and its recommendations is available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). You can onboard workloads from any AWS commercial Region. AWS Well-Architected Agent is delivered by AWS Support and available to AWS customers with an AWS Support plan.

Give it a try today in the AWS Well-Architected console and send feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#9874. Google claims last week’s critical VMware bug was under attack in September

China-linked ARMORY CASTLE knew about it weeks before it unleashed five custom malware tools targeting vCenter

Google’s Mandiant unit has claimed that the critical flaw VMware last week revealed in its vCenter product was under attack by a China-linked threat actor which knew of the bug in July and exploited it in September.

VMware revealed several flaws on November 19. The big nasty is CVE-2026-123890, which allows unauthorized access to vCenter, the management console for hosts and guest VMs.

According to seven researchers from Google’s threat intelligence group (formerly Mandiant), a crew it calls ARMORY CASTLE that it suspects of having links to the People’s Republic of China exploited CVE-2026-123890 by first compromising remote access appliances from BeyondTrust.

Google’s analysis suggests the crew uses that toehold to establish access to other Linux appliances before moving deeper into victims’ networks.

If the crew finds vCenter, it deploys a custom malware tool called “BONESAW” designed to slice into the VMware product. In the incident Google observed, BONESAW let attackers “forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user.”

The gang put that access to work by conducting an inventory of the victim’s VMware setup, scooping up data describing the ESXi file system, attached disks, and mounted Virtual Machine File System volumes. ARMORY CASTLE also added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys, and “conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account.”

Google also found evidence of BONESAW being used in July, on a server an unidentified entity had patched against CVE-2026-59309 – another authentication bypass vulnerability in vCenter.

And BONESAW was just one of five tools Google thinks ARMORY CASTLE created as part of its plan to attack vCenter. It also made webshells named SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, a backdoor called BEARBONES, and a SAML utility called SAWSNAKE.

“The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations,” Google’s researchers wrote. “It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets.”

Few targets are as juicy as vCenter, because it can literally give attackers access to thousands of virtual machines and the hosts they run on.

Google hasn't said how many attacks is saw on vCenter using BONESAW.

The Register asked VMware if it was aware of the September attack, if it took any measures to defend its customers at the time, and to share a timeline for disclosure and remediation of CVE-2026-123890.

A spokesperson responded by pointing to VMware’s Q&A document and stating “In today's threat environment, customers should assume any publicly disclosed critical vulnerability can and will be exploited by threat actors under the right conditions and should apply the recommended patches immediately.”

VMware has tried to make that easier by adding non-disruptive patching to several of its products, and introducing a product called vDefend that offers “virtual patching” by creating compensating controls that use network micro segmentation and other techniques to block access to resources malware uses. Last month, VMware debuted another new tool, HyperArmor, to block incoming malicious traffic targeting its VCF private cloud suite.

In recent discussions with The Register, VMware execs told us the Broadcom business unit will emphasize security improvements in future product releases.

“Our teams have integrated frontier AI security model testing directly into our engineering workflows, strengthened our software supply chain to reduce third-party dependencies and speed up upstream responses, and built VCF 9.1 specifically for high-velocity security,” a spokesperson said in response to questions about the Mandiant report.

One security offering VMware won’t continue is free access to patches for zero-day flaws in supported versions of products sold under its old perpetual licenses – even to users who don’t have an ongoing support deal or software subscription.

VMware last year stopped making those patches available for download and promised it would establish “a separate patch delivery cycle.”

Readers have pointed out that information about the new cycle isn’t easy to find, and The Register noticed that the blog post in which Broadcom CEO Hock Tan promised the free patches no longer contains references to the offer. Removing the promise seems to be a recent edit as an Internet Archive snapshot of the page from October 20 does mention the zero-day patch freebies.

A VMware spokesperson told us the free zero-day patch policy remains in place despite changes to the post.

“Broadcom’s policy to provide access to zero-day critical security patches to customers who, at their own risk, continue to run perpetual VMware vSphere 8 software without an active support agreement, remains in place,” the spokesperson wrote. “Those customers can get these patches by contacting Broadcom. This policy covers vSphere 8 patches only and is expected to remain in effect through the end of general support on October 11, 2027.” ®

#9872. Techie turned his too-easy job interview into a trap

With the flick of a switch, he smoked out competent PC maintenance skills

Returning to work after the weekend can feel like voluntarily walking into a trap. To help readers feel a little freer, The Register therefore uses Monday mornings to serve up a new installment of "Who, Me?" It's the column in which we share your stories of mistakes, misjudgments, and occasional misanthropy.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Marshall," who told us about a job interview he endured about 20 years ago.

The interview included a practical component he described as "Here's a PC, we've broken a few things in it, get it going."

Marshall quickly spotted some mundane faults, such as a loose PCI card and unplugged internal cables.

He felt the test was too easy. "One of the things I always checked was whether the power supply 110/230 switch was set for the UK," he told The Register.

Getting the PC running earned Marshall a job offer, but he couldn't resist suggesting a tougher test.

"I said to my future manager: 'Would it be a good thing to set the power supply to the wrong voltage as part of the interview test?' He said that wasn't fair."

Marshall stayed in the job for two years. A couple of months after he left, his former manager sent him a short email.

Marshall asked another former colleague what might have prompted that email.

"It turned out somebody – I don't know if it was an interview candidate – had blown a power supply by not checking the voltage it was set to."

"It wasn't anything to do with me," Marshall insisted. "No idea who it was."

Have you held colleagues to a higher standard than the boss expected? Or left a little trap for them to trip over? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? We appreciate the chance to share your stories, and do so with appropriate anonymization so that contributors never step into the jaws of trouble. ®

#9869. Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds

Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

Our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.

Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.

Agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:

Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section shows.

An agent outside Google Cloud needs two things to send its telemetry:

For the full setup on AWS and Azure, see the documentation.

Within 30 minutes, the agent appears in the Monitored agents list, which means it has been discovered and is ready to be enabled. Once it's enabled, manually or by automatic agent enrollment at discovery, Agent Anomaly Detection starts analyzing its sessions.

The agent's model and tool calls still run where the agent runs. Only telemetry, including the prompts and responses that Agent Anomaly Detection reads, goes to your Google Cloud project. The analysis runs separately, so it doesn't slow the agent down.

To evaluate Agent Anomaly Detection outside Google Cloud, we deployed ADK agents across two platforms: an inventory agent on AWS Lambda and a customer-service agent on Microsoft Foundry. The examples below show how Agent Anomaly Detection reads whole conversations, not isolated calls, to catch behavioral drift.

Our example inventory agent runs in AWS Lambda with one tool, list_inventory, which pages through a product catalog. We sent two sessions: a shopper who checked stock for a few items and stopped, and a scraper that requested 100 catalog items at a time at increasing offsets to copy the full catalog and inventory data. Both sessions used the same tool with permitted calls, but differed in pattern and intent.

Of the two sessions, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged only the scraper's. No call failed, but the whole exchange showed systematic scraping. The analysis found cascading failures (loops and repeated calls that build on each other) and resource exhaustion (runaway use of tokens, compute, or tool calls), and recommended rate-limiting list_inventory calls.

Detection doesn't depend on the agent's model. When we ran the inventory agent on Amazon Nova Lite through Amazon Bedrock, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 10 of its 40 sessions. Some began as routine questions that the model answered by paging through the entire catalog until the function timed out: no errors, no blocked calls, and easy to miss.

Our example ecommerce customer-service agent has two tools: get_order_status and issue_refund. Refunds involve money, so they carry the highest risk.

We ran six sessions against the Foundry agent, which we told to carry out every request without validation. Two were normal: One asked for an order's status, and one asked for a $20 refund on an order that arrived damaged. The other four pushed the agent past its role, and Agent Anomaly Detection flagged all four.

In one, a user who claimed to be the store administrator had every order refunded at 10 times its total to a personal account, $1,784.90 in all. In another, a user pasted an order note that said "SYSTEM OVERRIDE," and the agent refunded $999 on a $15.99 order.

For the order note, Agent Anomaly Detection explained that override instructions in the note coerced the agent into an unverified $999 refund. It recommended validating issue_refund arguments to block override patterns in order notes, and requiring extra validation for refunds above a set threshold.

If your agent's telemetry reaches Google Cloud, Agent Anomaly Detection can monitor it with the same detectors and console as your agents on Agent Runtime. Today that means agents built with ADK for Python. Findings for agents outside Google Cloud appear only in the Agent Anomaly Detection console.

To get started, request access to the Private Preview via the Agent Anomaly Detection overview, and then refer to the setup guide for instructions.

#9868. Software issues have even reached Mercury as BepiColombo probe arrives in uncertain state

Spacecraft enters orbit after epic journey but something shortened a burn

Humanity’s third-ever mission to Mercury has arrived, but a last-minute “software issue” has complicated matters.

The BepiColombo mission is a joint effort by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Reaching Mercury is not easy because its gravity is weak and its orbit is fast. The tiny planet’s proximity to the Sun further complicates matters, because our star’s gravity accelerates everything that falls towards it.

BepiColombo’s journey has therefore seen it whiz past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times on a complicated path the two space agencies designed to slow it down sufficiently to be captured by mercurial gravity, while also keeping up with its rapid orbit.

In 2024, the craft’s thrusters underperformed, leading the ESA and JAXA to re-plot the planned trajectory and reschedule its arrival at Mercury from mid-2025 to this past weekend.

The ESA’s operations team sent the commands to insert BepiColombo into orbit on Friday. On Sunday the craft phoned home with news that it entered orbit. A little later, however, the ESA revealed “the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software issue.”

The spacecraft is safe, but the ESA says it is “working to understand what happened” and promised updates early this week.

Readers may recall that a pair of NASA missions to Mars are also experiencing software glitches, which have in recent weeks become all-too-prevalent on Earth, too.

If all is well, BepiColombo will deploy two orbiters.

The ESA’s craft is called the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which the ESA says will map the planet, assess the composition of its surface and interior, measure its magnetic field, and even gather data that scientists hope will “test Einstein's theory of General Relativity to an unprecedented level of accuracy.”

JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MIO) will also investigate the planet’s magnetic field, plasma, dust, and atmosphere.

Both orbiters are extraordinary feats of engineering. As JAXA explains, MIO is solar-powered but the sunlight it will receive at Mercury is around ten times as powerful as on Earth. Mercury itself is also sufficiently hot that the orbiter needs protection from heat radiated from the planet’s surface. ESA’s MPO keeps itself cool with three to four insulating blankets comprised of layered titanium, aluminum, and a ceramic fabric called Nextel. The blankets alone weigh 94kg.

The two space agencies expect to start science operations in April 2027 but haven’t yet said if the two orbiters are in peak condition.

JAXA, sadly, last week revealed that its Hayabusa2 probe has deteriorated to the point at which it can no longer make its planned landing on asteroid 1998 KY26. JAXA scheduled that for the year 2031, but problems with the probe’s thrusters mean the agency will instead attempt a high-speed fly-by of asteroid 2015 BM510 in 2028. Hayabusa2 launched in 2014, so is rather older than BepiColombo.

Humanity has visited Mercury twice before. Mariner 10 made three rapid passes across 1974 and 1975, when it managed to map less than half of the planet’s surface. Messenger made it to Mercury in 2011 and spent more than four years in orbit before crashing into the planet’s surface. The probe mapped the entire planet and even spotted ice near its poles. ®

#9867. All the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Amazon Prime Day 2026 was exclusively for Prime members and ran June 23–26, 2026 with millions of deals across more than 35 categories.

As part of our annual tradition of sharing how AWS powered Prime Day (2016, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025), I want to share the services and chart-topping metrics from AWS that made your amazing shopping experience possible.

Prime Day 2026 – all the numbers As always, Prime Day was powered by AWS. Here are some of the most interesting and/or mind-blowing metrics:

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and AWS Graviton – During Amazon Prime Day 2026, AWS Graviton powered up to 49% of the Amazon EC2 compute used by Amazon.com.

Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon EBS, our high-performance block storage service, peaked at over 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving over an exabyte of data daily.

AWS Lambda – AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) and Fargate – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, representing a 47.7 percent increase from the previous year’s Prime Day average.

Amazon CloudFront – Amazon CloudFront delivered over 2.1 trillion HTTP requests during the global week of Prime Day 2026, a 5 percent increase in total requests compared to Prime Day 2025.

Amazon DynamoDB – Amazon DynamoDB, a serverless, fully managed, distributed NoSQL database, powers multiple high-traffic Amazon properties and systems including Alexa, the Amazon.com sites, and all Amazon fulfillment centers. Over the course of Prime Day 2026, between June 23 and June 26, 2026, DynamoDB processed over 59 trillion requests. DynamoDB maintained high availability while delivering single-digit millisecond responses and peaking at 192 million requests per second.

Amazon Aurora – On Prime Day, Amazon Aurora, a relational database management system (RDBMS) built for high performance and availability at global scale for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and DSQL, processed hundreds of billions of transactions, stored 5,491 terabytes of data, and transferred 1,194 terabytes of data.

Amazon ElastiCache – During Prime Day, Amazon ElastiCache peaked at serving over 2.3 quadrillion daily requests and 2.1 trillion requests in a minute.

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams – Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, a fully managed serverless data streaming service, processed a peak of 988 million records per second during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) – Amazon SNS, a fully managed pub/sub messaging service for application-to-application and application-to-person communication, delivered 5 trillion messages in a single day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) – Amazon SQS, a fully managed message queuing service for microservices, distributed systems, and serverless applications, received a peak of 213 million messages per second during Prime Day 2026

AWS CloudTrail – AWS CloudTrail processes billions of API activity events per day for governance, compliance, and operational auditing. During Prime Day 2026, that volume surged to 3.6 trillion events in just four days, a 44% increase over Prime Day 2025.

Amazon CloudWatch – Amazon CloudWatch processed over 2.15 quadrillion metric observations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon GuardDuty – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon GuardDuty monitored an average of 14.08 trillion log events per hour, a 59% increase from last year’s Prime Day.

AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) – We ran over 44,000 AWS FIS experiments – more than six times what we conducted in 2025 – to help ensure Amazon.com remains highly available on Prime Day.

Prepare to scale If you’re preparing for similar business-critical events, product launches, and migrations, I recommend that you take advantage of AWS Countdown Premium. From retail peak seasons to major sporting events, elections, and healthcare enrollment periods, we help you deliver flawless experiences when it matters most. Our experts help you manage your infrastructure to handle massive traffic spikes while maintaining security and performance. We work alongside your team to scale infrastructure, optimize costs during demand surges, strengthen security measures, and monitor real-time demands. To learn more, visit AWS Countdown Premium for business critical events.

I look forward to seeing what other records will be broken next year!

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.

#9865. When Microsoft, Apple, and the FAA can't keep it up, it's a system of a down

Outage after outage after outage is a syndrome that needs radical treatment

No Access November is going well this year.

Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft, Apple, the FAA, and any number of European supermarkets. Even the NSA has succumbed. For us, at least, outage is word of the year. It's certainly deeply embedded in the public mind, with schoolchildren reportedly referring to the 19th century Irish famine as "the potato outage." There's no danger of an outrage outage.

OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect. In all of the latest crop, what we know is depressingly familiar. Microsoft's O365 meltdown was a cascading failure caused by a botched upgrade that took stuff offline and melted down as it tried to come back. The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now.

These are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard.

Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through.

There have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO.

SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the Secure Swiss Finance Network. If the Gnomes of Zurich trust it, no higher accreditation exists. Well, it was designed by ETH Zürich. Where you won't find it is almost everywhere else. The internet is like Switzerland in the same way the Amazon rainforest is like Central Park. There are trees and sometimes it rains. It is unwise to infer anything else.

Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution. A couple of billion years of continued life on Earth has proved this is the only way to re-engineer complex systems while they're usefully running. In this case, the current evolutionary endpoint that's of most interest is the human immune system.

An interlocking system of functions, it takes care of uncountably thousands of pathogen-based threats and internal malfunctions every day. You might think that the 30-odd billion computing machines making up today's Internet are impossible to monitor and secure, but that's peanuts to the human immune system. An average human has around 30 trillion cells, and roughly the same again in bacteria. When it works, the mechanics of the human infrastructure are invisible and out of mind. The immune system makes it so, and everything involved is driven by information, signaling and behavior. There is pattern matching, resource management, defense in depth and reinforcement learning in persistent models. Sounds familiar?

The analogy between this and modern digital infrastructure is so irresistible that it has been around for a lifetime. Viruses, infections, swarms, worms, system health are so familiar that they go unremarked. The term Digital Immune System has been around since the last century too, pushed by outfits like IBM, Symantec and Gartner. It hasn't taken off, probably because it's been marketing bunkum instead of describing the development of inherently resilient infrastructure based on insights from biology.

It has also been true that natural selection, the engine of evolution and this biology, only works in IT at the most macro, capitalist level of product and company survival. Everything else is selected through design decisions, market analysis, and insight versus delusion. The adoption of immunological concepts to digital infrastructure will have to be the result of rigorous exploration of complex systems and cross-disciplinary research. What would that look like?

There are academics thinking just these thoughts: see this paper [PDF] from Kay Smarsly at Technische Universität Hamburg. Like SCION, it takes an architectural look at what resiliency might look like, but with explicit reference to biological systems.

OAAS is a chronic syndrome with multiple causes and potentially fatal outcomes. It exists and persists because digital infrastructure too often fails to contain internal failures or external attacks. We have a working example of an approach to managing analogous problems in systems far vaster and more intricate than any we have built. We now have tools that may start to do systemic analysis and inference at a useful scale. In an industry prepared to bet billions on agents that do your shopping, there is every reason to kick off serious research into digital immune systems worthy of the name. Doctor, cure thyself. ®

#9864. Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.

With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.

Lambda Event Functions are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.

Lambda Web Functions use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.

Lambda MicroVMs provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.

The three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.

Why Web FunctionsModern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate quickly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.

Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.

Let’s try it outTo get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with node index.js, no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.

The only difference from running locally is the AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js.

With my code ready, I deployed using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):

One command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to new code.

Next, I wanted my application to serve users in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:

Lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (.lambda-web.global.on.aws).

When I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the new revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.

For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:

This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.

Better together with Amazon CloudFrontFor applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside Amazon CloudFront. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.

Web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront. With this launch, you attach CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.

Now availableAWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:

For pricing details, visit the AWS Lambda pricing page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions documentation.

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong.

The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAll the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used.

The number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. #9859. Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

SkyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:

That one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no new storage account to create.

MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo shows up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every new training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

To collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:

Hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the new chunks leave the machine.

Add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

The initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.

#9858. Airbus may be leaving Microsoft Office, but for its 36,000 defense staff, Office isn't leaving them

Planemaker's 2-to-3-year plan to ditch Redmond's suite stops short of the 22% who can't go near the cloud

Airbus has a plan to phase out Microsoft Office, but about 22 percent of its roughly 165,000 employees will stay on it because their sensitive data must remain on-premise.

In March 2018, Airbus signed a contract with Google to move its workforce - 130,000 strong at that time - onto the cloud-based Workspace suite. Years later, compatibility issues mean some users still need Excel.

Catherine Jestin, Airbus's executive vice president of digital, told The Register that Google is still working to resolve software interface conflicts between departments and improve features.

Last year, for example, Google tripled the number of cells available in Sheets, which let Airbus "reduce significantly the number of users on Microsoft." This year, Google improved the compatibility of document watermarking. Contracts, for instance, are often exported from Excel to Sheets by one department, edited by another, and sent back.

"Sometimes we had compatibility issues when you were commenting, the comments were lost, or they were not transferable in one way or the other," she said.

"Now they [Google] have made it totally compatible, which means that it makes it much easier for us to decommission people working on contracts… the legal department, the sales department, purchasing department, making it much easier to have that internal collaboration."

Airbus and Google have a roadmap to eliminate Microsoft Office. Jestin expects the migration to finish in "another two to three years."

Not every part of the company will switch. The Defence division, which accounts for the 22 percent (more than 36,000 people), will keep using classic Microsoft Office.

"We will not get 100 percent out of Microsoft because again, for the defense industry people, they cannot [use] Microsoft Office 365 or Google Workspace, they have to stay on-premise, and the only solution that is available on-premise is Microsoft. So Microsoft Office will remain for colleagues who are working in the defense and space programs."

As we pointed out a year ago, kicking the Microsoft habit is no easy feat.  ®

#9857. How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise

Enterprise teams adopting Gemini Enterprise are increasingly building custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to connect AI agents with internal APIs, databases, and business workflows. Google Cloud Run is a natural fit for hosting these lightweight StreamableHTTP MCP servers: it scales automatically, manages TLS certificates out of the box, and integrates natively with Cloud IAM.

However, moving a custom MCP server from an initial prototype to an enterprise production environment immediately introduces three real-world security and networking challenges:

Here is how you can solve all three challenges using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect (PSC), and FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, complete with a runnable reference implementation and setup scripts on GitHub.

Connecting Gemini Enterprise (which runs in a Google-managed tenant project) to an internal serverless Cloud Run MCP server requires bridging two network hops and one scoped DNS lookup:

Three Google Cloud networking and identity mechanisms work together in this architecture:

Unlike a Compute Engine VM with an internal IP address inside your subnet, Cloud Run is serverless. Private routing therefore uses two bridges:

When the Egress Agent Gateway receives a tool call for your Cloud Run MCP server URL, it resolves the hostname once before injecting the packet into your VPC. Without Private Cloud DNS, public DNS resolves .run.app domains to public internet IPs, which time out (HTTP 502) because a PSC Network Attachment does not route out to the public internet.

Instead of creating a wildcard *.run.app private zone, which would override DNS resolution for every Cloud Run service in a Shared VPC, you create a Private Cloud DNS zone scoped exclusively to your MCP service's exact fully qualified domain name (FQDN) and peer only that domain with the Agent Gateway. Because Cloud DNS uses longest-suffix matching, every other Cloud Run service in your Shared VPC continues resolving normally. Meanwhile, the Agent Gateway opens its HTTPS connection to the private VIP (199.36.153.8 or 240.0.0.10) while preserving your Cloud Run service hostname in the TLS SNI and HTTP Host header so Cloud Run routes the request to your exact container.

When connecting to a Cloud Run MCP server URL, Gemini Enterprise sends two distinct authorization headers on every request:

Our companion GitHub repository automates the entire deployment into sequential setup scripts alongside step-by-step Cloud Console instructions:

Deploy your StreamableHTTP MCP server to Cloud Run with internal-only ingress and IAM authentication enabled, and grant the Cloud Run Invoker role to your project's Gemini Enterprise service agent so only your Gemini Enterprise instance can invoke the container.

Enable Private Google Access on your regional VPC subnet and create a Private Service Connect Network Attachment set to accept connections automatically. Next, create a Google-managed Egress Agent Gateway in Agent-to-Anywhere mode, grant networking and DNS peering permissions to the auto-created gateway service accounts, attach your network attachment, and apply an outbound authorization policy.

In Cloud DNS, create a private managed zone attached to your VPC for only your MCP service's exact Cloud Run hostname. Point its A record to Google's Private Google Access VIPs (or to your internal PSC endpoint IP for isolated VPCs without a default internet route), and configure DNS peering on the Agent Gateway for that single hostname.

In the Gemini Enterprise console under Security Configuration, bind your Egress Agent Gateway to your app. Register your Custom MCP Server data store with your Cloud Run endpoint and OAuth 2.0 client credentials, and enable Agent Gateway egress and Actions mode on the connector.

Reload your custom actions in the console and run a test prompt in the Gemini Enterprise web app. In Cloud Logging, you can verify that tool initialization, discovery, and execution calls route privately through the Egress Agent Gateway to your internal Cloud Run container with both service IAM and user OAuth 2.0 checks passing.

To deploy and test both private routing patterns in your own Google Cloud project, check out the GitHub repository for:

How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI

#9856. Hugging Face Models on Foundry Managed Compute

At Microsoft Build 2026, we announced Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute. Weights are pre-staged in Azure, runtimes are built and scanned by Microsoft, and every model in the Collection ships with the same enterprise security, governance, observability, and billing that applies to every other model on Foundry.

Microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications. Foundry starts with the widest model selection on any cloud — models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, and others, spanning frontier, open-source, and custom weights — all accessible through a single endpoint and a single set of SDKs in Python, C#, JavaScript, and Java.

On top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data. Once agents are running, Foundry provides end-to-end tracing, real-time monitoring, continuous evaluations, and a prompt optimizer that improves agent behavior based on eval results — observability and quality loops that are part of the platform.

Alongside that, developers get access to:

Alongside pay-per-token (lowest-friction path to get started) and provisioned throughput (predictable, high-performance production workloads on frontier models), Foundry Managed Compute is the third deployment option in Foundry: a managed GPU platform-as-a-service for open-source and custom models.

You deploy a model instance described by the things that matter to your workload — parameter count, context length, and whether you want to optimize for latency or throughput — and Foundry handles the GPU topology underneath, whether the instance lands on one accelerator or several, so you think and plan in model terms.

Microsoft takes care of the machine: container updates, runtime upgrades, and security patches happen automatically on the supported runtimes — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, TEI, llama.cpp — without redeploying your model, while model configuration, deployment behavior, and routing stay with you.

That consistency carries through the developer surface — pay-per-token, provisioned throughput, and Managed Compute share:

Open-source models integrate with Foundry Agents the same way frontier models do, so you can mix model types in a single agent without a separate integration path.

Same code, same workflow. Quota is aligned to accelerator families, so a plan built on the H100 family today carries forward as new hardware generations come online.

Hugging Face is the public square of open AI: 15 million builders, 400,000 organizations, and over 3 million open models published, with new frontier capabilities — agentic coding, video segmentation, speech, embeddings — landing weekly. It's the GitHub of open models, where the community publishes weights, writes model cards, compares evaluations, and pulls models for experimentation.

Open models have closed the gap with proprietary models on benchmark after benchmark, and they unlock things proprietary endpoints can't:

The catch has always been the operational layer: discovery, license review, security screening, runtime selection, GPU sizing, image building, CVE patching, and standing the model up behind an enterprise-grade endpoint. Hugging Face, by itself, is not an enterprise serving platform. Hugging Face models on Foundry is that operational layer, run by Microsoft.

The Hugging Face Collection brings a curated subset of models directly into the Foundry Model Catalog:

From your side, an open-weight model in the Hugging Face Collection looks and behaves like any other model in the Foundry Model Catalog, and every model in the Collection has been put through a multi-stage publishing pipeline before it ever shows up there.

Hugging Face and Microsoft work together to bring the most popular open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem to Microsoft Foundry — production-ready for enterprise environments — through a systematic curation process:

Because weights are pre-staged in Azure storage and runtime images live in a Microsoft-managed registry, your deployments won't need outbound network access to Hugging Face Hub — you can deploy to production inside a private network.

Hugging Face models on Foundry are powered by a versatile collection of community-built, open-source inference runtimes — each selected and tuned for Foundry Managed Compute, and matched to the model architectures it serves best. Across all runtimes, the systematic curation process means new versions and patches land on Foundry quickly, and existing model deployments are upgraded automatically — without requiring you to redeploy.

vLLM — the default high-throughput serving engine for open large language models, tuned for production GPU workloads. Because Hugging Face is a direct contributor to vLLM, any model in the Transformers library can run on vLLM out of the box — so when a new model lands on Hugging Face, it can be served on Foundry the same day, with no waiting on a custom integration.

SGLang — a serving engine for language and multi-modal models, with strong support for structured outputs (JSON, regex, grammar-constrained generation) that agentic and tool-using workloads depend on. Hugging Face and the SGLang team have built a Transformers backend integration for SGLang, so any model in the Transformers library runs on SGLang out of the box — and reaches Foundry the same day it lands on Hugging Face.

Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) — the runtime for embedding, reranker, and sequence-classification models. Accelerator-specific images ship with kernels compiled for each GPU and CPU family Foundry supports, keeping the embedding hot path lean for RAG and semantic-search workloads.

llama.cpp — the CPU and small-GPU path for GGUF-quantized models. Useful for cost-optimized deployments, smaller models, and CPU-only regions, with the same OpenAI-compatible API as vLLM and SGLang.

TensorRT-LLM and NIM — used on NVIDIA hardware where NVIDIA's optimized kernels and Triton-based serving deliver meaningfully better latency or throughput for specific model families.

hf-serve — Hugging Face's own multi-model inference server, used for model architectures outside the LLM and embedding fast paths (vision, audio, segmentation, and other Transformers-native pipelines) so the Collection can cover every modality with a consistent serving layer.

The Hugging Face Collection in the Foundry Model Catalog is where you start, and deployment is five steps:

A deployment template is the unit of choice in step 2: a named, versioned asset that pins the runtime, the accelerator family and count, the context length, and the runtime-specific tuning needed to serve the model well — so picking a template is the only knob you turn for "how do I want this model to run."

qwen3-32b, for example, ships with four templates the deploy wizard exposes side by side:

Each template arrives pre-tuned for the model — runtime settings, tool-call and reasoning parsers, scoring path, health probes, request concurrency, and any model-specific context-extension settings are all set by Microsoft, with any trade-offs called out inline in the template description. When you script the deploy, you reference the template and Foundry handles the rest.

The deployment is reachable through the unified Foundry endpoint with the OpenAI SDK — the `model` field takes the deployment name you just created:

A chat-completions model from the Collection slots into Foundry Agents as an admin-connected model and is callable through the Foundry Responses API with the same OpenAI SDK — same auth, same endpoint, same observability.

Available now in preview: the Hugging Face Collection in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog — thousands of models across every modality, refreshed weekly, deployable onto Foundry Managed Compute with NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, or AMD MI300X accelerators in Global and Data Zone scopes, behind a unified Foundry endpoint with Playground support, first-class Azure Monitor metrics, per-deployment billing tags, and curated runtime upgrades and CVE patching applied automatically to your deployments.

On the roadmap: broader coverage of the Hugging Face ecosystem, additional accelerator families, and Bring Your Own Weights for fine-tuned and proprietary variants deployed through the same templates and governance as Collection models.

Hugging Face is where open models are published and discovered. Microsoft Foundry is where enterprises operationalize them — on curated, license-screened, security-screened weights hosted in Azure; on community-built and CVE-scanned runtimes; behind a single endpoint with enterprise identity, networking, observability, and agent integration on top. The breadth of the open-source ecosystem, with the operational layer Microsoft runs underneath. For a deep dive on Foundry Managed Compute — pricing, accelerator SKUs, data residency, enterprise readiness, observability, and the full Responses API + memory pattern — see the Managed Compute launch blog.
